title: Rubio Announces Visa Curbs on South Africans Over Alleged Race-Based Discrimination
excerpt: The restrictions target those allegedly complicit in land seizures and discrimination against minorities; Pretoria says its apartheid-redress policies have been mischaracterized by fringe groups, and the U.S. ambassador hints at more measures to come.
body:
• Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a new visa restriction policy Tuesday targeting foreign nationals deemed responsible for or complicit in "race-based discrimination," uncompensated land seizures, or incitement of racial violence in South Africa.
  • No individuals have been named, and it remains unclear who will be affected; South Africa's foreign ministry says the move is based on a "mischaracterisation" of its policies by fringe groups.
  • The U.S. ambassador to South Africa called the restrictions "only the first step in a series of escalatory measures," as South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola travels to New York for the UN General Assembly.

Washington escalates pressure on Pretoria

The United States announced new visa restrictions on South Africans on Tuesday, escalating a diplomatic dispute that has been building since the start of President Donald Trump's second term. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the policy targets "foreign nationals who are responsible for, or complicit in, the enactment or implementation of laws or policies that enable uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination, and/or the incitement of imminent violence against members of minority ethnic or racial groups in South Africa."

https://x.com/SecRubio/status/2099968018272952511

"The South African government has not adequately addressed the previously laid out concerns," Rubio said in his statement, adding that the United States "will not allow such behavior to go unchecked" because the actions "directly undermine peace, economic stability, and the rule of law." He did not name any officials who would be penalized or identify anyone the restrictions would apply to.

Pretoria pushes back

South Africa's foreign ministry responded Wednesday, saying the announcement "aligns with the mischaracterisation of South Africa's domestic policies" by fringe groups. "It is our sovereign right to put in place laws that address the nation's concern over centuries of racial injustice," the ministry said, adding that bilateral challenges "can only be resolved by constructive engagement through state actors on both sides of the diplomatic channel, not unilateral acts."

The ministry's statement follows months of relative calm after a bruising 2025. Trump has repeatedly claimed — falsely, according to CNN's investigations, which found no evidence to support the assertion — that white South Africans face systemic persecution and even "genocide." In a meeting last year, Trump screened a video for President Cyril Ramaphosa in the Oval Office that he said documented anti-white persecution; Ramaphosa replied that the speeches shown "are not government policy" and that South African policy is "completely, completely against what he was saying."

Domestic financial markets shrugged off the announcement: the rand was little changed at R16.27 to the dollar on Wednesday afternoon, while the yield on benchmark 2036 bonds eased three basis points to 8.93%.

More measures signaled

The visa restrictions may be only the beginning. The U.S. ambassador to South Africa posted on X on Wednesday that they were "only the first step in a series of escalatory measures," declaring that "the time for endless 'dialogue' has run its course" and that the consequences "are necessarily going to be severe."

The timing is delicate: South Africa's Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola was en route to the United States on Wednesday to attend the UN General Assembly in New York, setting up a possible confrontation in person.

Context: a widening rift

The restrictions are the latest in a series of actions targeting South Africa. The administration has already created a special refugee pathway for Afrikaners: an emergency presidential determination in May raised the refugee admissions ceiling from 7,500 to 17,500 for fiscal year 2026, citing "grave humanitarian concerns" over alleged racial violence by the South African government and political leaders. The policies Washington objects to are land reform and affirmative action measures that South Africa says are necessary to remedy the legacy of apartheid — policies under which white South Africans remain, on average, far wealthier and more likely to be employed than Black South Africans.

Impact and what's next

For travelers and workers, the immediate practical effect is uncertain until Washington names targets. But the episode fits a broader pattern of nationality-based immigration restrictions from the administration — worth watching for diaspora communities worldwide, including Indians who study and work in South Africa and the roughly 1.5 million people of Indian origin who call the country home. If the ambassador's warning holds, escalation could follow the General Assembly meeting. South Africa, for its part, is betting that sustained diplomatic engagement can still defuse the standoff.
